analysis.one_liner: Expands the Supreme Court from nine justices to thirteen.
analysis.headline: The bill to expand the Supreme Court from 9 to 13 justices drew only 3 of 100 senators as supporters and never left the Senate Judiciary Committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal law so the Supreme Court has a Chief Justice and 12 associate justices instead of 8, and it would raise the number of justices needed for a quorum from 6 to 8. Supporters argue a 13-seat Court would dilute the current 6-3 conservative majority, which resulted from appointments made by presidents who lost the popular vote and a seat blocked in an election year. The bill went nowhere: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the immediate beneficiary is whoever holds the White House and Senate at the time of confirmation — three new seats. Supporters argue ordinary Americans would benefit over time from rulings shaped by a more ideologically varied Court on issues like abortion, voting rights, labor law, and regulation. Critics say the main beneficiary is the Democratic Party's litigation agenda.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Supporters of a rebalanced Supreme Court

how_it_helps.text: Raises the Court from 9 to 13 seats, allowing three new justices to be appointed.
Raises the quorum from 6 to 8 justices, so a smaller rump of the Court could not decide cases alone.
Supporters argue this would rebalance a Court whose 6-3 conservative majority does not reflect the country, affecting rulings on rights and protections ordinary people rely on.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund three additional justices' salaries and staff — a trivial cost. The larger cost, according to critics, is to the Court's perceived independence: if one party adds seats when it can, the other party can add seats when it can, making every future justice confirmation a raw power contest.

drawbacks.text: Critics across the political spectrum call this court-packing: changing the number of justices to get desired outcomes, which risks a cycle in which each party adds seats whenever it holds power, permanently politicizing the Court.
The bill's benefits to ordinary people are indirect and contingent — they depend entirely on how future nominees rule once confirmed, unlike a wage floor or drug price cap whose effects are direct.
With only 3 Senate supporters out of 100 and no House companion momentum, the bill had no realistic path, so its sponsors spent political capital on a symbolic measure rather than achievable reform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real grievance — that the current Court's majority was shaped by contested appointment circumstances — but it does so through a mechanism that invites retaliation from the opposing party and that commanded almost no support even among Senate Democrats. Its practical effect as introduced was symbolic.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Sen. Ed Markey introduced the bill on May 16, 2023.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee that same day, which was its last action of record.
Two other Senate Democrats cosponsored it; no Republican did.
The bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo prevailed: the current 9-justice Court and its 6-3 conservative majority remained intact, which is the outcome opponents of expansion preferred. Because the bill died without a vote, neither its supporters nor a voting public ever got a judgment on the merits — the Democratic chair of the committee simply never acted on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The current 9-justice Court stayed as is

for.name: Sen. Ed Markey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three Senate supporters were Democrats (Markey plus 2 of his 48 Democratic colleagues), no Republican supported it, and the Democratic committee chair declined to move it — a Democratic proposal that most of the Democratic caucus also did not back.

industries.industry: Political parties and court-focused advocacy groups
industries.note: The bill is a fight over which party's appointees control the Supreme Court, not over any industry. Whoever held the presidency and Senate at confirmation time would have gained three seats; no business sector is directly affected.
